extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of international maritime law; readers of legal history
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the rules and principles governing neutral commerce, seizure, contraband, blockades, right of search, convoy, and armed neutrality in wartime maritime law. Focuses on what may be seized, when, and the legal consequences for neutrals and belligerents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seizure of enemy effects on neutral ships
rubrics_metrics.description: If enemy property is found on board a neutral ship it may be seized by right of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captors are naturally bound to pay the freight to the master of the vessel, 'who is not to suffer by such seizure.' Risk exists that the voyage may be interrupted by seizure of hostile property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restoration of neutral effects found in enemy ships
rubrics_metrics.description: Neutral goods found in an enemy's ship are to be restored to their owners; there is no right of confiscation against neutrals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restoration is required 'but without allowance for detainder, decay, &c.' Neutrals who voluntarily place goods in a hostile ship expose them to such accidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutral jurisdiction does not protect enemy property beyond neutral limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Neutral ships do not afford protection to an enemy's property when that property is beyond the limits of the neutral jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated as 'a clear and well-settled principle of the Law of Nations.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Captor's entitlement to freight when completing voyage
rubrics_metrics.description: When a captor carries goods to the port of destination he is entitled to the freight, standing in the place of the owner of the ship and performing the specific contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the captor does not proceed to perform the original voyage, he is not entitled; exception exists when goods are carried to his own country or ports to which they would have been consigned if not prevented by regulations of the country of embarkation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freight allowance to captor when goods carried to captor's country
rubrics_metrics.description: Freight will be allowed to the captor even though he carries goods to his own country, and to the ports to which they would have been consigned if not prevented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under certain circumstances the captor is considered entitled to freight even though the goods are carried to his own country and restored; however, if the captor injures the property or is guilty of misconduct he may be answerable by way of set-off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability for captor misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: If the captor injures the property or is guilty of misconduct, he may remain answerable for the effects of such misconduct as a set-off against him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces or defeats freight or prize claims when misconduct affected the value or condition of goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: No belligerent rights on public neutral vessels at sea
rubrics_metrics.description: No right of visitation and search, capture, nor any other belligerent right can be exercised on board a public neutral vessel on the high seas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with private vessels, which 'form no part of neutral territory' and when within another state's limits are subject to local jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutral master entitled to reasonable demurrage when bona fide
rubrics_metrics.description: If a neutral vessel having enemy goods on board is taken and the neutral master's conduct is fair, he will be entitled to reasonable demurrage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The captor pays the whole freight because he represents the enemy; neutral master must have acted bonâ fide and with strictly neutral conduct. (Note: 'This Rule Changed by Convention'—treaties may alter.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty rule: 'free ships make free goods'
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern practice often stipulates by treaty that 'free ships shall make free goods' meaning neutral ships protect neutral goods by convention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such treaty stipulations may change historical rules; the converse ('enemy's ships make enemy's goods') is sometimes subject of treaty but not necessary in general law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutral goods on armed belligerent vessels (divergent national rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions (e.g., United States) protect neutral goods on armed belligerent vessels, while others (e.g., England per Sir Wm. Scott) hold that putting goods on a ship of force betrays intention to resist search and withdraws neutrality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sir Wm. Scott's test: if the neutral 'puts his goods on board a ship of force, which will be defended by force, he betrays an intention to resist visitation and search.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of purchases of enemy vessels by neutrals
rubrics_metrics.description: Purchase of enemy ships by neutrals is permitted provided the transfer is bonâ fide and absolute, divesting the enemy of all interest; conditional sales or arrangements preserving enemy interest vitiate the sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sales under condition to reconvey at war's end, or sales where the seller is under penalty to not sell (but purchaser exonerates him), have been held invalid. Purchases of ships 'built for war' raise special questions and may require superior court authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contraband classification (three classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contraband generally includes warlike stores and articles directly auxiliary to war; writers distinguish (1) things useful only for war, (2) things not so, and (3) things of indiscriminate or dual use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First class excluded from neutral trade; second generally admitted; third depends on circumstances (quality, quantity, destination). Examples: money, provisions, ships, naval stores are sometimes lawful and sometimes not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articles ipso facto contraband when destined for besieged places
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain articles become contraband ipso facto if carried to a besieged town, camp, or port.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a specific rule regardless of their normal classification in peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naval materials and ships as contraband in naval war
rubrics_metrics.description: In a naval war ships and materials for ships are contraband, even if the raw materials (timber, cordage) can be used for other purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment depends on quality, manufacture, or quantity relative to war circumstances; if it's highly unlikely they are intended for non-warlike use, they may be contraband.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisions generally not contraband except to besieged/blockaded places
rubrics_metrics.description: Common provisions are not contraband under general prize law, except when sent to a besieged or blockaded place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical controversy existed (e.g., British suspicions re: trade to France), but treaty practice often limits contraband to military/naval stores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaties may enumerate contraband; effect limited to parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Nations often enumerate contraband articles in treaties to remove doubt; such treaties bind only the nations that are parties to them and do not operate as general law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently neutrals not party to a treaty are not bound by its contraband list except by their own agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Destination and port character as tests for contraband (Lord Stowell)
rubrics_metrics.description: The destination (military or commercial port) and the character of the port are material facts: goods destined for a naval equipment port are presumptively for hostile use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Undeveloped or raw materials may get indulgence (e.g., iron vs anchors); but naval stores may be contraband irrespective of port if inherently meant for naval use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigated exercise: purchase/pre-emption instead of confiscation for provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Belligerents sometimes exercise a right of pre-emption (purchase at reasonable compensation and fair profit) for provision cargoes instead of full confiscation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neutral owners can expect reasonable compensation, not the enemy's famine price; this is treated as a 'mitigated exercise of war.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Contraband penalty limited to cargo unless aggravating circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Under modern law, contraband cargo generally affects only the cargo (loss of freight and expenses), not the ship; condemnation of the ship requires aggravating circumstances or owner connection with contraband.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggravations include false destination, false papers, or transfer of contraband by neutral between ports for war purposes — these may extend taint to vessel and justify condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer of contraband within neutral ports treated as importation
rubrics_metrics.description: Transfer of contraband by a neutral from one port of a country to another, when required for war purposes, is treated the same as original importation into the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents neutrals from legally re-exporting contraband within the enemy state to avoid liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return voyage proceeds generally protected
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, the proceeds of the return voyage cannot be taken; the offence is complete when quitting port on a hostile destination but penalty not held to attach beyond capture if not in delicto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If goods are not taken 'in delicto' and not in actual prosecution of such a voyage, later seizure may not attract penalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transporting enemy's forces forfeits neutral vessel
rubrics_metrics.description: A neutral vessel hired or used to convey the enemy's military persons is to be considered a transport and is subject to condemnation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number alone is not decisive; importance and rank of persons (e.g., a single veteran general) can make the act sufficiently hostile. Pressed service does not exempt the vessel; the master cannot aver involuntary agency as a defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carrying enemy despatches grounds for condemnation
rubrics_metrics.description: Carrying the enemy's despatches is treated as an act of the most hostile nature and grounds for forfeiture of the ship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despatches may convey campaign plans; confiscation of the papers would be meaningless, so the vehicle (ship) is forfeited. Exception: despatches of an ambassador or public minister resident in the neutral country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three elements to constitute breach of blockade (Lord Stowell)
rubrics_metrics.description: To constitute a violation of a blockade three things must be proved: (1) the existence of the blockade; (2) knowledge of it by the party accused; and (3) some act of violation (entering or leaving, or loading after commencement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intention to evade and overt acts toward the port are fraudulent breaches; timing of shipment (before or after blockade commencement) is material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for lawful maritime blockade (presence and sufficiency of force)
rubrics_metrics.description: A lawful maritime blockade requires the actual presence of a sufficient force stationed at the entrance of the port, sufficiently near to prevent communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blockade continues despite occasional absence due to winds; if blockading squadron is driven off by superior force, blockade is lifted and must be renewed by fresh notification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standard for blockade and effect of notification
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of a blockade must be clear and decisive; a declaration alone unsupported by fact is insufficient. There are two kinds of blockade: simple (blockade in fact) and blockade in fact with notification—notification affects presumed duration until revoked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a neutral country is remote and lacks constant information, vessels may lawfully conjecture blockade has been broken after a long time; treaties may require 'warning off' neutrals before they are held to know of the blockade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maritime blockade not violated by land/internal carriage
rubrics_metrics.description: A maritime blockade is not in law violated by bringing or sending goods to the port through internal canal navigation or land carriage of the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such goods are therefore not liable to confiscation on ground of the blockade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of visitation and search on the high seas
rubrics_metrics.description: Belligerent cruisers lawfully have the incontestable right to visit and search merchant ships on the high seas, whatever the ship, cargo, or destination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interposition of a neutral sovereign's force cannot legally vary that right; violent contravention of the right may be punished by confiscation of the property withheld from visitation and search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convoy and insurance warranty to sail with convoy
rubrics_metrics.description: Convoy is warship escort for merchant vessels; insurance policies commonly warranty that the vessel shall sail with convoy, failing which insurance may be void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warranty requires sailing with the convoy from the appointed place of rendezvous (not necessarily immediate port of lading) and continuing under protection unless prevented by tempest or unavoidable accident; master must seek sailing orders from the convoying squadron. Statute may prohibit sailing on a foreign voyage without convoy except by license.

rubrics_metrics.name: Armed Neutrality principles (five-point statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles historically proclaimed by Russia and other powers: (1) commerce with enemy ports free to neutrals; (2) the ship covers the cargo; (3) contraband only as declared by treaty; (4) a place not blockaded unless surrounded so no person can enter without manifest danger; (5) these principles to guide prize legality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These principles were adopted by several European powers and the United States as a basis to resist certain belligerent practices; belligerents (e.g., Great Britain) disputed them as inconsistent with generally acknowledged Law of Nations or prior treaty engagements.
